closest_papers.title: Beyond Token Savings: A Systematic Study of Context Compression in LLM Agents (Satish, Sinha, Kawada, Yadwadkar)
closest_papers.what_it_answers: The removal arm, on almost exactly the student's setup: mini-swe-agent, vLLM, three open-weight models (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Devstral-Small-2-24B, GLM-4.7-Flash), 100 SWE-bench Verified issues plus 40 Terminal-Bench tasks, 3 runs each, about 35,000 runs over 65 policies. On Qwen, clearing tool results leaves the resolve rate about where full context is (53.7% vs 53 of 100 solved); across policies compression changes SWE-bench success by between -11.0 and +0.7 points, and policy rankings reverse between models.
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: No arm adds context, none targets failed tool output specifically, and failed vs successful run lengths are not compared. The authors say the cross-model reversals need 'further controlled analysis'. Removal from step 0 changes the whole trajectory, so it does not isolate context size at a fixed state.

closest_papers.title: Switch-SWE: Do Coding Agents Hold Focus When Switching Between Unfinished Tasks? (Chang et al.)
closest_papers.what_it_answers: A forward, matched-pair intervention on coding agents: 200 focus tasks, each run uninterrupted and with stages of four other unfinished same-repo tasks interleaved. Focus-task resolution drops by 11.5 points on average (6.0 to 15.0) across 7 agent configurations.
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: The added context is real work on other tasks, so length is confounded with task interference and cross-task confusion. No padding control, no dose variation (one schedule of four interruptions), single runs without intervals, API-served frontier models in vendor harnesses, not SWE-bench Verified. The paper itself says token usage cannot separate the effects.

closest_papers.title: When and How Context Rot Appears in Coding Agents: A White-Box Study of Agent Skills in Code Auditing
closest_papers.what_it_answers: A direct context-addition test on a coding agent with everything else held fixed (Codex, gpt-5.4-mini, one code-audit workflow): clean context passes 8/10, about 299K characters of relevant or irrelevant added context passes 3/10 each. It finds no stable dose threshold ('Raw length alone is insufficient').
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: n=10 per arm, Fisher p=0.07, sample extended after seeing pilot results, 28 of 57 extension attempts excluded, one task and one closed model, context added up front rather than as accumulated tool errors, dose roughly 75K tokens rather than 20-35K. Not SWE-bench, no open model in the main experiment.

closest_papers.title: LOCA-bench: Benchmarking Language Agents Under Controllable and Extreme Context Growth
closest_papers.what_it_answers: An experimenter-set dose-response for tool-using agents with task semantics held fixed: 15 seed tasks at 8K to 256K tokens of environment data, 75 samples per length. Accuracy falls steeply for every model, e.g. Claude-4.5-Opus 96.0 to 14.7, DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking 78.7 to 6.7, Kimi-K2-Thinking 74.7 to 2.7.
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: Workflow tasks (email, spreadsheets, databases), not repository repair. The added content is task data the agent must process, so length is confounded with task difficulty. No intervals. Models are frontier or very large; nothing at 30B. Says nothing about whether failing runs merely run longer.

closest_papers.title: Evaluating Long-Context Reasoning in LLM-Based WebAgents (Chung et al.)
closest_papers.what_it_answers: The forward injection design the card says is missing, on web agents: irrelevant trajectories injected between two dependent subtasks to reach 25K to 150K tokens, with a no-noise baseline. Success falls from 40-50% to under 10% (GPT-4.1 44.4% to 2.7%, o4-mini 46.2% to 21.2% at 150K).
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: Web tasks on live sites, 56 tasks, task requires retrieving a fact from before the injected block (so it tests retrieval across noise as much as length), per-length numbers only in figures, one open model (Llama 4 Maverick) capped at 75K. Not coding, not error output.

closest_papers.title: Causal Decomposition of LLM Agent Failure via Oracle-State Intervention (Jia et al.)
closest_papers.venue_year: NeurIPS 2026 workshop poster (Who Verifies the Agents?)
closest_papers.what_it_answers: Already in the card for the reverse arm (replacing context after failure recovers under 10% of 420 failed WebArena runs; 11.7% of failures attributed to context). The abstract also reports a forward arm the card omits: continuously maintained oracle state raises success by 19-38%, with the gap over self-generated state growing from 8% to 12.5% as trajectories lengthen. Uses Qwen3.5-27B and GPT-5.2.
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: WebArena only; replaces history with structured ground truth rather than varying its volume; no coding tasks. Read from the NeurIPS abstract page only (OpenReview was behind a browser check).

closest_papers.title: Compact-Bench: Measuring What Context Compaction Costs Long-Horizon Coding Agents (Sun et al.)
closest_papers.what_it_answers: A same-state paired replay on SWE-bench repairs: after at most 10 steps, continue from full history or from a summary with the same repository snapshot. Defines 'rescue' (full history fails, summary passes); the first-round outcome table shows none, while 5% to 64% of 22 full-history successes are damaged depending on summarizer.
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: Built to measure compaction damage, not harm from accumulation: 35 repairs, fork after only 10 steps (little accumulated context), 8-step continuation, one continuation agent (Kimi-K3), no aggregate rescue count, no relation between history size and outcome.

closest_papers.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Context Rot in Long-horizon Search (Xia, Wang, Huang, Liu)
closest_papers.what_it_answers: For search agents on open models (GLM-4.7, GLM-5.0, Qwen3.5-397B, MiniMax-2.5): accuracy drops with trajectory length, and keeping only the last 3 turns 'almost completely eliminates the rot phenomenon' at the cost of more unfinished runs. A length-threshold sweep gives rot rate 2.4% / 7.2% / 20.2% at 32K / 48K / 64K.
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: Removal only, no injection, search not coding. The authors' own limitations say it is unclear whether results generalize to software development. Does not address selection (struggling runs accumulate more).

closest_papers.title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories (Zhao et al.)
closest_papers.what_it_answers: Observational support for the 'symptom' reading: in 1,184 failed Terminal-Bench runs (7 models incl. open-weight, 3 scaffolds incl. MiniSWE), the decisive error has a median onset at step 7 against a median failed-run length of 27 steps, i.e. within the first quarter, before most context has accumulated. False premises are the largest trigger (30.7%); output misreading is 4.4%.
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: Manual annotation, no replay or counterfactual, and context length is not analysed at all.

closest_papers.title: The Limits of Long-Context Reasoning in Automated Bug Fixing (Raju et al., SambaNova)
closest_papers.what_it_answers: Replicates the correlation on the student's exact setup (mini-SWE-agent, 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, open models): Qwen3-32B averages 8,854 tokens on passed vs 17,627 on failed runs; DeepSeek R1 8,538 vs 15,554. Also shows single-shot patching at 64K context collapses (Qwen3-Coder-30B 7%).
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: Correlation only for the agentic arm; the long-context arm is single-shot, not a live trajectory. Note the trajectories stay under about 20K tokens, so the card's 20-35K padding dose would more than double the context for this harness and model size.

closest_papers.title: The Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs (Sinha et al.)
closest_papers.what_it_answers: A controlled injected-history experiment that separates length from error content on a synthetic running-sum task: with an error-free history, turn-100 accuracy is already below turn-1 (length effect); raising the injected error rate lowers it further (self-conditioning). Qwen3 thinking models do not show the self-conditioning effect. Tested on Qwen3 4-32B and Gemma3 4-27B among others.
closest_papers.what_it_leaves_open: Synthetic task, no tools, no coding. The agentic part is a manual re-read of existing failure annotations, not an experiment.

answered.summary:
Verdict: partly answered. The exact experiment on the card has not been published as far as I could find, but the card's claim that no forward test exists is too strong, and one of its three arms is already run. My search was cut short by the web-search budget, so treat "not found" as weaker than usual.

What the card missed:
- **Forward injection exists in neighbouring settings.** Web agents drop from 40-50% to under 10% when irrelevant trajectories are injected up to 150K tokens (arXiv 2512.04307). Workflow agents fall from 64-96% to 3-21% as environment data grows from 8K to 256K (LOCA-bench, 2602.07962). A Codex code-audit task goes from 8/10 to 3/10 with about 299K characters of added context, though at p=0.07 (2607.17937).
- **A coding-agent forward test appeared ten days ago.** Switch-SWE (2611.02017) uses matched pairs and finds an 11.5-point drop, but the added context is real work on other tasks, with no padding control and no dose variation.
- **The masked arm is essentially done on the student's setup.** "Beyond Token Savings" (2609.32961) runs mini-swe-agent on vLLM with three open-weight 24-35B models on SWE-bench Verified, about 35,000 runs. Clearing tool results leaves Qwen's resolve rate about level with full context, and compression overall moves success by -11.0 to +0.7 points.
- **Evidence already leans toward "symptom" at natural context lengths.** The decisive error in failed Terminal-Bench runs has a median onset at step 7 of 27 (2607.09510). Compact-Bench's same-state replay shows no rescues from dropping history (2610.31710), and Jia et al. recover under 10% by repairing context.

What is still open is the padded arm: error-like text at the 20-35K dose, on SWE-bench trajectories, with a model near 30B. A reviewer could reasonably predict the result from the above: little effect at that dose, clear harm only at 100K and beyond.

One practical point for the first experiment: on mini-SWE-agent with Qwen3-32B, runs average about 9K tokens when passed and 18K when failed (2602.16069). The card's 20-35K dose comes from a different harness and would more than double this context.

evidence_checks.claim: IISWC 2026 workload paper: failed runs carry more context; authors propose error output as the mechanism; one configuration has the sign reversed (Gemma Instant, SWE-bench Pro, 82.2K successful vs 72.3K failed).
evidence_checks.note: All quotes and numbers are in v2 (Sec. on Fig. 6): 79.2K vs 44.4K for Qwen Thinking on Terminal-Bench, the 'failed Bash, Edit, or Read actions append error messages, stack traces, failed patches' sentence, and the 82.2K vs 72.3K exception. Caveat on meaning: the stated mechanism explains why failed runs end up with more context (failed tool calls add error text and more turns). It is the symptom direction, not a claim that context causes failure. The paper says so itself right after the exception: 'This suggests that large context is not inherently a failure mode.' It also documents a failure-driven retry loop (Gemma Instant on ADE, Edit failing 95.4%, up to 786 turns). Models are Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma4-31B under Claude Code, served by vLLM. arXiv comment field says IISWC 2026, so the venue is author-stated, not only inferred.

evidence_checks.claim: Complexity Trap: removing context changes solve rate with opposite signs across models (Gemini 2.5 Flash thinking 40.4/36.4/31.4; Qwen3-32B thinking 23.0/24.6/24.8; Gemini 2.5 Flash 32.8/35.6/36.0), and the paper does not account for the difference.
evidence_checks.note: Numbers match Table 1 (n=500, SWE-agent, SWE-bench Verified). Caveat: only the Gemini 2.5 Flash thinking drops are significant in the paper's paired bootstrap (Table 4: masking -4.0 pp [-7.8, -0.2], p=0.04; summary -9.0 pp, p<0.0001). The positive changes are within noise (Gemini Flash +2.8 pp [-0.8, 6.4], p=0.15; +3.2 pp, p=0.09; Qwen3-32B thinking +1.6/+1.8 pp against a CI of about +/-3.8). The card omits two of the five configurations: Qwen3-32B non-thinking 17.0/15.0/16.0 (negative, not significant) and Qwen3-Coder 480B 53.4/54.8/53.8 (flat). So 'opposite signs' is one significant drop against four nulls. Each configuration is a single run at temperature 0.8. I found no explanation of the Gemini thinking drop in the text, so 'does not account for' looks right. The paper's own summary is that context management reduces cost 'without significantly reducing solve rate'. The intervention also removes old observations, so it changes information content and trajectory length together with context size.

evidence_checks.claim: Jia et al. (NeurIPS 2026 workshop poster): 420 failed WebArena trajectories; replacing context after failure recovers under 10%; annotators attribute 11.7% of failures to context.
evidence_checks.note: All three numbers are in the abstract on the NeurIPS page (workshop 'Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development'; models Qwen3.5-27B and GPT-5.2). Caveat: the card leaves out the other half of the same abstract. 'continuous oracle state throughout the trajectory improves success by 19-38%, and the gap between oracle-maintained and self-generated state widens from 8% to 12.5% as trajectories lengthen.' That is a forward-direction intervention showing that context quality maintained throughout matters a lot, on web tasks. The abstract also opens with 'LLM agents degrade as trajectories lengthen'. So this paper does not simply support the 'context is a symptom' reading. Only the abstract was read; the full paper (OpenReview YwrRO2qfsr) was not opened.

evidence_checks.claim: Token-consumption paper: 'higher token usage does not translate into higher accuracy; instead, accuracy often peaks at intermediate cost and saturates at higher costs.'
evidence_checks.note: Quote is in the v2 abstract/intro and still in v3 (2 Oct 2026). Basis: each task run four times, runs ranked by cost; accuracy rises from the cheapest to the next run and then saturates. Caveats: the quantity is total billed tokens per run, not context length at a given step; models are eight frontier LLMs, not 30B open models; within a task the costlier runs are not clearly worse (saturates), which fits 'symptom' at least as well as 'cause'. The paper itself attributes the across-task negative correlation to task difficulty and ties expensive failed runs to repeated view/edit of the same file. v2's text is inconsistent in one place ('degrades at the highest cost levels'). No venue found in the arXiv record.

evidence_checks.claim: IISWC paper: 'Failed agents often carry larger contexts (up to 1.8x in terms of mean) and longer tails'.
evidence_checks.note: This is the Fig. 6 caption, verbatim. Same paper as the first item, so it is not independent evidence.

evidence_checks.claim: IISWC paper leaves dynamic context compaction or summarization out of scope.
evidence_checks.note: Verbatim in the limitations paragraph: 'Advanced orchestration techniques, including speculative or overlapped tool execution, dynamic context compaction or summarization, and branching or tree-search workflows, are outside the scope of this study.'

evidence_checks.claim: Complexity Trap: 'LLM-Summary consistently leads to longer trajectories, suggesting they mask failure signals that would otherwise prompt earlier termination.'
evidence_checks.note: Verbatim in the Figure 4 caption. Section 4.4 adds 'context summaries act as a reinforcing signal, encouraging the agent to keep going.' Exception stated in the paper: for Qwen3-32B it was masking, not summarization, that lengthened trajectories (13%). Venue per arXiv comment: DL4C workshop at NeurIPS 2025 (camera-ready, v3). Note this quote treats error output as useful signal, which cuts against the card's proposed 'masked' arm being a pure context-size manipulation.

evidence_checks.claim: Copilot trace paper: sessions with at least one compaction event are 7.8% of sessions and 44.2% of total tokens; no quality signal ('Without prompt/response content, we cannot correlate infrastructure efficiency with task completion quality').
evidence_checks.note: Numbers are in Table 6 and the surrounding text; the limitation sentence is verbatim. Caveat: the card's title is wrong. The paper is 'Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale' (Liu, Qiu, Goiri, Fonseca, Bianchini, Choukse; 30 Jul 2026). This item only shows the absence of a quality signal; it adds nothing on causality.

premise.is_tension_real:
Partly. The gap is real in its narrow form, but the "conflict" between sources mostly dissolves on reading.

- **IISWC does not assert the causal claim.** Its mechanism runs from failing tool calls to more context, and it states that "large context is not inherently a failure mode". The card's question is one the paper raises only by implication.
- **The "opposite signs" in Complexity Trap are one significant drop against four nulls.** Only Gemini 2.5 Flash thinking moves significantly (-4.0 and -9.0 pp); the other four configurations, including both Qwen3-32B ones, are within noise. The card shows three of five configurations and none of the significance markers.
- **The sources measure different things.** IISWC is context at end of run by outcome (Claude Code, 27-31B open models, five benchmarks). Complexity Trap is a whole-policy change that removes old observations and also changes trajectory length. Jia et al. is post-failure replacement with oracle state on WebArena. The token paper is total billed tokens across four reruns on frontier models. None of them holds the state fixed and varies context size.
- **Jia et al. is quoted selectively.** The same abstract reports that continuous oracle state improves success by 19-38%, with the gap widening as trajectories lengthen. That is evidence that context quality matters in the forward direction.

The gap statement ("no paper adds context in a controlled dose to a coding agent and measures solve rate") survived the checking I could do, but that checking was thin: the session's web-search budget ran out after one query. The nearest work I found or already knew, opened by arXiv ID:
- SWE-Explore (2606.07297, Sec. 4.4): pads a patcher's context with random non-core code, n=150, GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4-mini. Redundant context costs 7-9 pp only when core evidence is absent and is tolerated once it is present. This is a single-shot patcher, not a multi-turn trajectory.
- Sinha et al. (2509.09677): injects a controlled error rate into the model's history and finds per-step accuracy falls with it, beyond the pure length effect; thinking models are reported as unaffected. Synthetic task, with only an anecdotal agentic appendix.
- Du et al. (2510.05381): length alone, even whitespace padding, degrades single-shot performance 13.9-85%, including coding tasks. Abstract only.
- SWE-ContextBench (2602.08316): a search summary says a full raw prior trajectory in context gave 27.27% vs 26.26% with none and 34.34% with a summary. I did not verify these numbers in the paper.

A 2026 paper doing exactly the forward-dose test on coding agents could exist and I would not have found it.
premise.obvious_answer:
An expert would predict "both, with the symptom direction dominating", with fairly high confidence on direction and less on magnitude.

- **Symptom direction: near-certain by construction.** Context grows monotonically with turns. Successful runs stop at submit; failed runs continue into retry loops or the turn limit. IISWC documents this directly (Gemma Instant on ADE, Edit failing 95.4%, up to 786 turns), and the token paper attributes high-cost failures to repeated view/edit cycles and task difficulty. Most of the 1.8x gap is expected to be duration and selection.
- **Causal direction: a small negative effect.** Padding 20-35K tokens of unrelated stderr into a ~30B model's trajectory should cost a few points at most. Basis: Complexity Trap (removing roughly half the context moves solve rate by under 3 pp, not significant, in four of five configurations, including Qwen3-32B); SWE-Explore (irrelevant code tolerated once the needed evidence is present); Du et al. and the context-rot literature (length and distractors hurt somewhat, more for smaller models); Sinha et al. (thinking models largely immune to errors in history).
- **Consequence for the first experiment.** The predicted effect is at or below the roughly 8-point resolution the card states for 100 tasks, so the likely outcome is an uninformative null.

Two things keep this from being fully obvious. The magnitude for 27-32B open models at 60-100K tokens is not pinned down by any of these sources. And a padded run that approaches the context limit (Qwen3-32B needed YaRN to reach 122K in Complexity Trap) would fail for a mechanical reason that has to be separated out.

The proposed padded arm also tests irrelevant distractor text from other tasks, which is not the IISWC mechanism (the run's own error output, which Complexity Trap treats as a useful failure signal).
premise.summary:
Q26's premise is weakened: every quote and number on the card is in its source, but the tension is thinner than the card presents.

- **Evidence accuracy.** All eight items check out against the primary pages (arXiv HTML for 2605.26297, 2508.21433, 2604.22750, 2608.00101, and the NeurIPS poster page). One bibliographic error: the Copilot paper's real title is "Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale". Two items are the same IISWC paper counted twice.
- **IISWC does not make the causal claim.** Its mechanism explains why failed runs accumulate context, and it says outright that "large context is not inherently a failure mode".
- **"Opposite signs" is mostly noise.** In Complexity Trap only Gemini 2.5 Flash thinking changes significantly (-4.0 and -9.0 pp); the other four configurations are nulls, and the card omits two of them (Qwen3-32B non-thinking 17.0/15.0/16.0 and Qwen3-Coder 480B 53.4/54.8/53.8).
- **Jia et al. is quoted selectively.** The same abstract reports that continuous oracle state improves success by 19-38%, which is forward-direction evidence that context quality matters.
- **The narrow gap looks real but is weakly checked.** I found no forward dose-response test on a multi-turn coding agent, but the web-search budget ran out after one query. Adjacent work covers pieces of it: SWE-Explore's noise injection into a patcher's context, Sinha et al.'s controlled error rate in history, and Du et al.'s length-only padding.
- **The answer is largely predictable.** Mostly symptom, with a small causal harm of a few points, which is below the roughly 8-point resolution of the proposed 100-task experiment. The searcher's own note in harvest_question_papers.md (line 217) already says the masking result leaves this "partly answered".
- **The first experiment does not test the stated mechanism.** It pads with unrelated stderr from other tasks, which is a distractor test, not a test of the run's own error output.

feasible.first_week_experiment:
**Day 1, CPU only: does the anomaly exist in this harness?**
- Data: the Complexity Trap trajectories (HF dataset JetBrains-Research/the-complexity-trap, Apache-2.0, 22.5 GB tar.gz; SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified n=500, includes Qwen3-32B raw).
- Measure: context tokens at matched turn index for resolved vs unresolved runs, tokens added per turn, and the share of observation tokens that are error output (non-zero return code, tracebacks).
- Comparison: is the failed-minus-successful gap made of more tokens per turn (the IISWC mechanism) or only more turns (the symptom reading)?
- Also download and inspect the IISWC trace (figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.33188042, CC BY 4.0). I could not open it today (HTTP 403), so whether it holds content or only token counts is unknown.

**Days 1-2: harness setup**
- mini-swe-agent (MIT) with `mini-extra swebench --subset verified --split test -w N`, pointed at a local `vllm serve`.
- Environment class: `singularity` with apptainer 1.4.2 (installed; subuid range present for `--fakeroot`), or rootless Docker.
- Write a padding hook of about 50 lines: wrap the environment's `execute()` to append filler to the returned output. The stock observation template cuts outputs over 10,000 characters to head 5,000 plus tail 5,000, so the pad must go outside that truncation.
- Scoring: sb-cli, or the local swebench harness (needs a Docker daemon).

**Models**
- Primary: Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 (Apache-2.0, cached). One model per card, thinking on, model-card sampling (temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95), `--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 --watermark 0.1`, prefix caching on, bf16 KV, `--max-model-len 200000`. The 402K-token pool gives about 6 concurrent agents at 60K context, or 2-3 in the +100K arm.
- Replication: Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 (Apache-2.0, block FP8, about 29 GB, to download; it is the IISWC model). The 199K-token pool gives about 3 agents per card at 60K. Run the +30K arms only.

**Arms** (same 100 Verified tasks, stratified by repo, paired by task)
1. Raw.
2. Raw again with a different seed. This A/A run gives the flip rate, which is the noise floor.
3. +30K tokens of stderr from other tasks' failed runs, spread over tool calls. This is the natural failed-minus-successful dose.
4. +100K of the same, an oversized dose.
5. +30K of neutral filler (benign log lines), to separate length from error-like content.
6. Masked: failed tool outputs cut to 200 tokens.

Then rerun arms 1, 3 and whichever of 4 or 5 is most informative on all 500 tasks with the MoE model.

**Number measured**
- Paired solve-rate difference vs raw with a paired bootstrap 95% interval, read against the A/A band.
- Turns per run, exit status (submitted, step limit, context overflow), and prefix-cache hit rate, to confirm no arm was thrashing.

**Power**
- If 15-25% of tasks flip between two runs, the 95% half-width is about ±9 points at n=100 and about ±4 points at n=500.
- The card assumed a 17-25% solve rate. That is outdated: Vals.ai (snapshot 2026-09-01, mini-SWE-agent, 500 tasks) lists Qwen 3.6 27B at 70.0%. The local FP8 solve rate is unknown until arm 1 runs.
feasible.result_that_kills_it:
Any of these means stop:

1. **Day-1 trajectory analysis**: at matched turn index, resolved and unresolved runs carry the same context and the same error-output share, so the gap is entirely "failed runs take more turns". The motivating anomaly then does not exist for SWE-bench-style coding runs. The IISWC paper itself reports the reversed sign on SWE-bench Pro for Gemma Instant; its 1.8x gap is on Terminal-Bench and GAIA under Claude Code.
2. **Intervention null**: +30K error text, +30K neutral filler and +100K all sit inside the A/A band (interval within about ±4-5 points at n=500) with unchanged turn counts. That is the "symptom" answer, which the Complexity Trap (masking vs raw on Qwen3-32B: -2.0 points, CI [-5.0, 1.0], p=0.21) and the under-10% oracle-repair recovery already point to. It makes a short negative note with no serving mechanism to build.
3. **Effect only at the oversized dose**: a drop at +100K with nothing at +30K is generic long-context degradation, not the accumulated-error mechanism, and that is already a known literature.

A fourth early stop is practical: if arm 1 on the local FP8 models lands above about 85% or below about 15%, the benchmark has no room to show a paired effect at this size.
feasible.result_that_makes_it_a_paper:
A monotone dose-response with a drop of at least 5-8 points at the natural dose (+20-35K), clearly outside the A/A band at n=500, replicated on both models. It gets stronger if any of these also hold:
- Error-like padding hurts more than neutral filler of equal length (content, not length).
- The masked arm recovers part of the loss.
- Padded runs take more turns before failing.

To carry a full paper it would still need two things beyond week one:
- A forked-state version: replay recorded runs to turn k, inject the pad, and continue with several seeds.
- A replication where the 1.8x gap was actually observed: Claude Code through Harbor on Terminal-Bench 2.0, which needs a Docker daemon and is a heavier setup.

Sign heterogeneity that tracks something measurable (thinking on vs off, as in the Complexity Trap's Gemini split, or model family) would also be publishable, but it needs more arms than week one holds.

Even the positive result is an agent-evaluation finding. The systems contribution would have to come from the follow-on.
feasible.gpu_days_first_week:
About 4-6 GPU-days, on the 3 cards idle at check time (GPUs 2, 5, 6; cards 1, 3, 4 had 15-29 GB used by others). That is roughly 2 days of wall-clock once the harness works.

Breakdown:
- Six arms x 100 tasks on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8: about 1-1.5 GPU-days.
- Three arms x 500 tasks on the same model: about 2-2.5.
- Three arms x 100 tasks on Qwen3.6-27B-FP8: about 1.5.
- Pilot and debugging: about 0.5.

These are estimates, not measurements. They come from the student's decode step times and an assumed 30K output tokens and 50 turns per task (Vals reports 1.44M total tokens per task for Qwen 3.6 27B). No agent run has been timed on this node. Container CPU time and disk, not GPUs, are the likely limit.
feasible.blockers:
1. **No agent harness exists.** mini-swe-agent, swebench and the padding hook must be installed or written; allow 1-2 days.
2. **Containers.**
   - The Docker daemon is not running. Rootless Docker binaries are in /home/ryankert_l/bin and worked in 2025-09 (28 GB of old images in ~/.local/share/docker).
   - Apptainer 1.4.2 is installed. mini-swe-agent's singularity class builds a writable sandbox per instance under the temp dir, so TMPDIR and APPTAINER_CACHEDIR must be redirected.
3. **Disk is nearly full.** Free space: / 19 GB, /home 35 GB, /share2 93 GB. /share1/saves is world-writable with 401 GB free but is not the student's directory, so ask first. SWE-bench Verified images run to tens of GB or more; I did not verify the size today.
4. **Scoring.** The local swebench harness needs Docker. The alternative is sb-cli cloud scoring, which needs an API key and uploads patches; I did not re-verify it today.
5. **Image pulls.** 100-500 pulls from Docker Hub need a logged-in account because of rate limits.
6. **Statistical power.** n=100 resolves only about 9 points; the decisive contrast needs all 500 tasks, and local FP8 solve rates are unknown.
7. **External validity.**
   - The IISWC gap was measured with Claude Code via Harbor on two H100s and is largest on Terminal-Bench and GAIA.
   - mini-swe-agent already truncates observations at 10K characters, so the natural error-accumulation mechanism is muted in this harness.
8. **Shared node.** 96 cores and 251 GB RAM are shared; 15-20 concurrent containers running test suites will be visible to other users.
9. **Limits of this check.** The web-search budget ran out partway through. I did not recheck novelty, the IISWC figshare contents (HTTP 403), or Qwen3.6-35B-A3B's mini-SWE-agent score; its model card states 73.4 on an internal scaffold.

No licence, model-size or engine-feature blocker: both models are Apache-2.0, fit one 48 GB card at FP8 with 200K context, and need nothing beyond vLLM 0.32.
feasible.follow_on_design_space:
**If context is causal (positive):**
- Context hygiene becomes a serving problem. Masking or deduplicating failed tool output mid-history breaks the prefix cache, so the mechanism to build is cache-preserving compaction: where to cut so the KV prefix (and, for hybrids, the recurrent-state checkpoint) survives. This is the student's existing strength.
- Context growth rate becomes a scheduler signal with a causal reason: admission and preemption that favour sessions whose context is still clean, or that trigger compaction before thrash.

**If context is a symptom (negative):**
- Context management buys cost only. The systems question reduces to GPU-seconds at fixed accuracy: eviction and compaction policies judged on cost, with no accuracy claim.
- Growth is still a failure predictor, so a scheduler could deprioritise or stop sessions predicted to fail. That space already has a neighbour: AgentStop (arXiv 2605.15206) does early termination from token log-probabilities, so the remaining room is the serving-side policy, not the predictor.

Either way the engine work is a second project; the first-week result itself contains no serving mechanism.
feasible.summary:
Q26 is answerable on this node, and more cheaply than the card assumed, but nothing has been run: the estimates below rest on the student's step-time measurements and public numbers, not on an agent run.

- **What changed from the card**: its power worry assumed a 17-25% solve rate (Qwen3-32B, 2025). Vals.ai's 2026-09-01 snapshot lists Qwen 3.6 27B at 70.0% on SWE-bench Verified with mini-SWE-agent. The cached Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 decodes about 5x faster than the 27B and has a 402K-token KV pool on one card, so all 500 tasks per arm are affordable (about ±4 points paired).
- **Cost**: about 4-6 GPU-days in week one. GPUs are not the limit; containers and disk are.
- **Real blockers**: no agent harness in the repo, no running Docker daemon (apptainer and rootless Docker binaries are present), and disks at 98-100% full.
- **Weakest point of the design**: the 1.8x failed-vs-successful gap was measured with Claude Code via Harbor, mostly on Terminal-Bench and GAIA, and the same paper shows the reversed sign on SWE-bench Pro for one configuration. mini-swe-agent also truncates observations at 10K characters. A CPU-only check on the public Complexity Trap trajectories (context at matched turn, resolved vs unresolved) should come first; it can kill the question in a day.
- **Likely outcome**: the existing evidence (masking vs raw at -2.0 points, p=0.21; under 10% recovery from context repair) leans toward "symptom". A null at +30K and +100K would confirm the expected answer and leave nothing to build.
- **Paper outcome**: a clear dose-response at the natural dose on two models, with error-like text worse than neutral filler, followed by a forked-state test and a Terminal-Bench replication.

My web-search budget ran out mid-check, so I did not recheck novelty and could not confirm image sizes, sb-cli, or the contents of the IISWC trace.

gaps.missing: Structured output and constrained decoding (grammar/JSON-schema masks, tool-call arguments). No card covers it. The practitioner-disputes harvest set aside 'structured output versus reasoning quality' as 'appeared to have a published answer (from memory, not re-verified here)'. The published answers actually disagree, and every one of them was measured at batch size 1 on non-thinking models.
gaps.why_it_matters: Tam et al. (EMNLP 2024 Industry, arXiv 2408.02442) report that format restrictions lower reasoning accuracy. JSONSchemaBench (arXiv 2501.10868, fetched) reports the opposite on Llama-3.1-8B: GSM8K 80.1% unconstrained versus 83.7-83.8% with XGrammar or Guidance, and a per-token time of 6.37 ms with Guidance versus 15.40 ms unconstrained, but states 'The batch size is set to 1 for all experiments'. CRANE (ICML 2025, arXiv 2502.09061) takes the accuracy loss as given and fixes it by leaving reasoning unconstrained. On the systems side, the vLLM blog says synchronous mask computation blocks the whole batch, and a vLLM pull request found threading the mask only pays above about 128 structured requests per batch (search results, not opened). This is a contradiction plus a batch-1 assumption in exactly the student's strengths (vLLM internals, reasoning benchmarks), and almost every agent tool call goes through this path.
gaps.example_question: For open thinking models served on vLLM, where the grammar applies only after the thinking block, does constrained decoding still change answer accuracy (Tam et al. say it falls, JSONSchemaBench says it rises by about 3 points), and does the per-token speedup JSONSchemaBench measured at batch size 1 turn into a throughput loss at the batch sizes a 48 GB card holds because the CPU-side mask computation stalls the whole batch?

gaps.missing: Theory versus measurement as a kind of tension, and 'open problems' lists as a source. The search used one classic queueing result (closed versus open loop, Q11) but did not mine the 2025 queueing-theory papers on LLM serving, whose stated model assumptions are directly testable. Mitzenmacher and Shahout's 'Queueing, Predictions, and LLMs: Challenges and Open Problems' (arXiv 2503.07545, also a SIGMETRICS 2025 tutorial) is an explicit open-problems list naming KV memory limits and the choice of preemption approach; it was not used.
gaps.why_it_matters: Li, Dai and Peng (arXiv 2504.07347, fetched) prove that work-conserving schedulers (fill every batch to the token limit) are throughput-optimal and conclude that vLLM with chunked prefill is throughput-optimal. Their model states '(Our model has completely ignored the memory constraint.)' and does not model preemption; KV memory for long-context or test-time workloads is listed as future work. The student's own measurement contradicts the conclusion in the memory-bound regime: holding back admission with a 0.05 watermark cut preemptions 15-25x and step time by about 17% (no MTP), which means a less work-conserving policy served more. A theorem with a named missing constraint and a measurement that violates it is a cleaner tension than most harvested cards, and both answers are useful (either the theory needs a memory term or the 17% is an engine artifact).
gaps.example_question: When KV memory rather than compute caps the batch (long reasoning outputs on a 48 GB card), is a work-conserving scheduler still throughput-optimal as Li, Dai and Peng prove for a model without a memory constraint, or does maximum throughput require deliberately leaving batch slots empty, and by how much does the optimal admission level sit below 'full' as output length grows?

gaps.missing: Simulator versus real system. No card tests a serving simulator. The word 'simulator' appears in the notes only for the student's own D2 cache simulator. Vidur (MLSys 2024), LLMServingSim 2.0, TokenSim and the 2026 Vidur extension KernelSight-LM (arXiv 2606.28565, search result only) were not harvested.
gaps.why_it_matters: Configuration searches, autoscalers and several scheduling papers are evaluated in simulators whose fidelity was validated on chat-length workloads. LLMServingSim 2.0 (arXiv 2602.23036, abstract fetched) claims it reproduces performance, memory and power 'with an average error of 0.95%'; Vidur claimed under 9%. Cascadia's own simulator reports 2-7% error. The student has measured effects that profile-based simulators typically do not model: preemption and recompute under KV pressure, the watermark setting, prefix-cache thrash, per-request recurrent state on hybrids. A fidelity study in the memory-bound reasoning regime is feasible on A6000s (the search summary said LLMServingSim 2.0 was validated on RTX A6000 and H100 with vLLM; I did not confirm that in the paper), and the result either licenses simulator-based papers for this regime or shows which mechanism they lack.
gaps.example_question: Does a profile-based serving simulator that reports about 1% average error (LLMServingSim 2.0) keep that error on vLLM 0.32 when long reasoning outputs make the batch memory-bound and the engine preempts and recomputes requests, and if the error grows, which unmodelled mechanism (preemption recompute, prefix-cache eviction, hybrid recurrent state) accounts for it?

gaps.missing: MoE-specific behaviour under batching. MoE appears in only 4 of 35 cards and only through speculative decoding (MoESD). No card asks how expert sparsity itself changes with batch size, although the student already has baseline runs for Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B in results/profile/harness/done/.
gaps.why_it_matters: Several top-ranked cards (Q03, Q02, Q01, Q22) turn on the batch occupancy at which an engine moves from memory-bound to compute-bound. For MoE models that crossover is not the dense one. MoE-CAP (arXiv 2412.07067v6, fetched) states 'the sparsity of MoE systems is closely influenced by the batch size' and measures that at batch size 8 already 53.05%, 46.79% and 18.44% of parameters are activated for DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Qwen1.5-MoE and DeepSeek-R1; it also says its bandwidth metric 'is only meaningful in memory bandwidth-bounded scenarios'. So the per-token weight-read saving that defines an MoE shrinks as the batch fills, at a rate that depends on how tokens share experts. Nobody has tied this curve to serving decisions on current A3B-class models, and the 2026 open models people actually deploy on 48 GB cards are increasingly MoE.
gaps.example_question: For Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on a 48 GB card, at what batch size does the union of experts activated per decode step saturate so that the model reads as many weights per step as a dense model, and does that saturation point (rather than the KV size) predict where batch-dependent results measured on dense models, such as the speculative-decoding break-even or the parallel-chains crossover, move for MoE?

gaps.missing: Energy and power as the cost metric. Every card counts cost in GPU-seconds, tokens or requests per second. 'Energy' occurs in the notes only in the sense of 'low-energy directions' of a state matrix. On-device and constrained hardware is absent too (Kinetics' own 'left open' note about local deployment was recorded but not carded; Intelligence per Watt, arXiv 2511.07885, was not harvested).
gaps.why_it_matters: 'Where Do the Joules Go?' (Chung et al., arXiv 2601.22076, fetched; 46 models, 1,858 configurations, vLLM 0.11.1, H100 and B200 only) finds reasoning uses about 25x more energy per response than chat, partly because 'higher energy per token due to memory pressure limiting batch size', and that energy per token 'drops at first, then plateaus' with batch size. It explicitly leaves the main knob untested: 'While not explored in this paper, GPU power limit' shapes the time-energy frontier. In the memory-capped regime the student has characterised, the GPU is under-utilised, which is the condition under which a power cap should cost little throughput. This needs only nvidia-smi power limits and the existing harness, and extends to a different GPU class (A6000) than the paper covers.
gaps.example_question: When long reasoning outputs cap the batch by KV memory so the GPU sits below compute saturation, how far can the GPU power limit be lowered before tokens per second fall, and does that make the energy-optimal operating point for reasoning workloads differ from the throughput-optimal one that 'Where Do the Joules Go?' treats as equivalent?

gaps.missing: Diffusion language models. One incidental mention in the notes, no card. All 35 questions assume autoregressive decoding (dense or GDN hybrid). A 2026 serving literature now exists: Sangam (arXiv 2607.04206), dLLM-Serve (arXiv 2512.17077), Optimus (arXiv 2605.24832), DiLaServe (arXiv 2606.29094) and an IISWC 2026 characterisation from Virginia (the last four seen in search results only).
gaps.why_it_matters: This is a regime shift with the same shape as the cards the judges ranked highest (a batch-1 claim that may not survive load). Vendors claim 4-10x single-request speedups over autoregressive models. Sangam (fetched; H100, LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B versus Llama-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B) measures that 'For both dLLMs, iteration time grows several-fold across the measured range, while for the AR models it grows only modestly' and concludes decode batching is 'significantly less impactful' for diffusion models, but it does not report a head-to-head throughput comparison under load, and bidirectional attention rules out chunked prefill and exact KV caching. LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B fit a 48 GB card. The answer decides whether diffusion LLMs are a latency product only or also a throughput product.
gaps.example_question: At what concurrency on one GPU does a diffusion LLM's single-request speed advantage over an equal-size autoregressive model turn into a lower tokens-per-second-per-GPU figure, given Sangam's measurement that diffusion iteration time grows several-fold with batch size while autoregressive iteration time grows only modestly, and is the crossover set by the diffusion model being compute-bound from batch 1?

gaps.missing: Multi-model serving on fixed hardware: routing, cascades, and co-located models. 'Router' and 'routing' occur zero times in the notes. Every card studies one model on one engine (the only two-model card, Q22 on SpecReason, is a draft-verify pair). The 2026 vision paper from the vLLM Semantic Router project (arXiv 2603.21354, abstract fetched), which lists 'twenty-one concrete research directions', was not used; no vision paper or keynote list was.
gaps.why_it_matters: Cascade and router papers report large gains but under conditions a single-node deployer does not have. Cascadia (arXiv 2506.04203, listed as ICLR 2026 in search results; fetched) claims up to 5x (2.4x average) higher throughput than single-model deployment, evaluated on 32 H100s with DeepSeek 7B/70B/671B and Llama 8B/70B cascades, quality scored by GPT-4o as judge, and the paper does not state the GPU count given to the single-model baselines. On a fixed 4-card node, splitting cards between models thins each model's batch (losing the batching efficiency the student has measured), and escalated queries pay twice. Q04 asks 'think longer versus bigger model' but as a static choice; the per-query routing version, with thinking budget as a third arm, is uncovered.
gaps.example_question: On a fixed node of four 48 GB GPUs, does a small-to-large cascade of the kind Cascadia reports as up to 5x faster on 32 H100s still beat the best single model given all four cards at full batch occupancy when quality is exact-match on reasoning benchmarks rather than an LLM judge, or does splitting the cards and re-running escalated queries cancel the gain, and does routing between thinking budgets of one model beat routing between models?

gaps.missing: Multimodal serving (image, video, audio inputs). 'Multimodal' occurs zero times in the notes. Not covered: encoder cost, visual-token count as the context-length driver, visual-token pruning as the multimodal sibling of KV eviction. Related serving work exists (ModServe, SoCC 2025, arXiv 2502.00937; HeteroServe arXiv 2603.12707 and TCM-Serve arXiv 2603.26498, search results only).
gaps.why_it_matters: The same 'does the gain survive a batched engine' question that produced the search's best KV-compression cards is open here with a ready-made critical paper. Wen et al., 'Token Pruning in Multimodal Large Language Models: Are We Solving the Right Problem?' (ACL 2025 Findings, arXiv 2502.11501, fetched) state 'FLOPs are not a reliable metric for evaluating speed gains', show SparseVLM with 2.8% more FLOPs than FastV but 26.8% more latency, and find random and pooling baselines beating designed methods on most benchmarks; they give no batch size, hardware or serving engine. Search summaries say ModServe found the image encoder can dominate time to first token (up to 79% for cross-attention models; not confirmed in the abstract). If the encoder and prefill dominate, pruning inside the LLM may buy little throughput until KV memory binds. Lower priority than the others because it is furthest from the student's current harness.
gaps.example_question: On a batched engine serving a current open vision-language model, does visual-token pruning raise requests per second at all before KV memory caps the batch, given that Wen et al. show FLOPs do not predict latency and random pruning matches designed methods, and is whatever gain remains explained by the number of tokens removed alone rather than by which tokens the method selects?

critic.biases_in_ranking:
Counts are from questions_ranked.json unless noted.

1. Toward the student's existing harness and dropped directions. 28 of 35 cards declare overlap with dropped directions D1-D4, and most 'first experiments' reuse the oracle@k harness, the D2 cache simulator or the D3 profiling curves. The feasibility judge (doable on 4x 48 GB in a month) rewards exactly this, so the ranking partly measures 'already instrumented' rather than 'important'.

2. Toward reasoning models and one model family. 19 of 35 question texts mention reasoning or thinking, 10 mention agents, 7 hybrids; 33 of 35 cards mention Qwen, 26 mention 48 GB, 23 vLLM, 18 AIME. The top seven are all reasoning-length or agent or hybrid questions. Chat, embedding, multimodal, MoE-as-such and diffusion workloads are absent.

3. Toward one question shape: 'does a published gain survive a batched engine, a stronger baseline or a deployer's metric'. This is a re-measurement or negative-result shape. It scores well with the skeptical reviewer and on feasibility, but the 'opens a solution space' score reaches 5 on only three cards. Lens averages show it: regime_shifts 4.05, stale_baselines 3.10 (lowest), with noise and replication cards (Q08, Q13, Q35) at the bottom. Constructive questions (what mechanism or design would work) are almost missing.

4. One cost metric. Cost is always GPU-seconds, tokens or requests per second on a single engine. No energy, no tail-latency-under-SLO question as the primary variable, no multi-model or multi-tenant setting, no simulator.

5. Source skew. arXiv is mentioned 743 times; ML and NLP venues dominate (ACL 117, NeurIPS 104, ICLR 56) over systems venues (NSDI 29, OSDI 18, ASPLOS 4, SOSP 3, EuroSys 1). Four workshop items, no keynote or open-problems list, no vision paper, no award paper, no theory paper beyond one classic queueing result. Industry material is vLLM issues and model cards rather than tech reports.

6. Set-asides made from memory. Several topics were dismissed without a check: 'structured output versus reasoning quality ... (from memory, not re-verified here)', and provider-to-provider variance on the strength of one article. At least the first is wrong as stated (gap 1). The pipeline-versus-tensor-parallelism item (OSDI 2026) was set aside as answered although the note itself lists an open residue (vLLM, reasoning-length outputs, MoE and hybrids) that matches the student's four PCIe-connected cards.

7. Architecture assumption. Every card assumes autoregressive decoding on a dense or GDN-hybrid model with text input; the memory-bound versus compute-bound crossover that drives the top cards is treated as a property of the engine, although it differs for MoE and diffusion models.
critic.summary:
I read all 35 question lines in /home/ryankert_l/kv-fetch/kv-fetch/research_notes/Research question search/questions_ranked.json, the lens and overlap fields, and the set-aside sections of the nine harvest_*.md files, then searched the web for each candidate gap. Nothing was modified.

The search is deep but narrow: reasoning-length outputs, KV compression, speculative decoding, scheduling, agent prefix caching and hybrid numerics, almost all on one autoregressive Qwen model on one vLLM engine, costed in GPU-seconds. Eight gaps, most important first:

1. Structured output and constrained decoding: dismissed from memory, but the papers disagree on accuracy and all measured at batch size 1.
2. Theory versus measurement: a 2025 proof that work-conserving scheduling is throughput-optimal ignores memory, and the student's watermark result contradicts it; open-problems lists were not mined.
3. Simulator versus real system: simulators claiming about 1% error have not been tested in the memory-bound, preempting regime.
4. MoE under batching: expert sparsity shrinks as the batch fills, which moves the crossovers the top cards depend on.
5. Energy and power: the main 2026 measurement study leaves the GPU power limit untested.
6. Diffusion language models: batch scaling is measured as much worse than autoregressive, with no head-to-head under load.
7. Multi-model routing and cascades on a fixed node.
8. Multimodal serving and visual-token pruning.

Gaps 1-4 fit the student's hardware and skills most directly; 2 and 4 can start from data already in the repo.

Areas I checked and did not card: multi-LoRA and fine-tuning systems (ForkKV, arXiv 2604.06370, reports that LoRA switching breaks KV reuse; search result only), on-device inference (Intelligence per Watt, arXiv 2511.07885), cache-sharing side channels and privacy (zero mentions in the notes), and the tensor-versus-pipeline-parallelism residue. Determinism and reliability are reasonably covered (Q13, Q29, Q34).

Verification: for each gap's source I opened the arXiv abstract or HTML page through a summarising fetch, so quoted phrases may be slightly paraphrased. Items marked 'search result only' or 'not confirmed' were not opened. The fetch tool refused to return full abstracts verbatim, so numbers come from its extraction of the paper body.
